596.title: Head on the arm
596.hook: a quiet prayer of confession, head resting on the arm, left out on happy days
596.howItsDone: On ordinary weekdays, after the morning and afternoon Amidah, many Jews say Tachanun, in many Ashkenazi communities resting the head on the forearm; it is omitted on Shabbat, festivals, Rosh Chodesh, Hanukkah, Purim, all of Nisan, Tisha b'Av and in other joyful circumstances.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last words of the Amidah: my God, guard my tongue. Your line was let my soul be like dust. Today, the Amidah is over, and the service goes somewhere lower.

A weekday morning service, a minute after the Amidah ends, can look like a room full of tired students. People sit down, lean forward, and rest their foreheads on their forearms, like a kid with their head down on the desk. The room goes quiet. Nobody's asleep. They're saying a prayer that's meant to be said from that low place. And on some days, the happiest ones, the whole thing is simply skipped.
screen: `HEADS DOWN, LIKE STUDENTS AT DESKS.` → `NOBODY'S ASLEEP.` → `SKIPPED ON HAPPY DAYS.`

segments.voice: It's called Tachanun, supplication, pleading. Its oldest form is nefilat apayim, falling on the face. In the Bible, Moses and Aaron fall on their faces before God; so does Joshua, after a defeat. In the time of the Talmud, people seem to have stretched out on the ground. Today, in many Ashkenazi communities, it's become the head resting on the arm; many Sephardi communities say it sitting, without lowering the head. The words are honest and low. One line, from King David, is said in many communities just before. In the old Jewish translation: "let us fall now into the hand of the LORD; for His mercies are great; and let me not fall into the hand of man." David has done wrong and is given a choice of punishments. He chooses God's hands over human hands, because, he says, His mercies are great. Then, in the Ashkenazi rite, Psalm 6: I am weary with my groaning. Here's the surprising part. Tachanun is left out on joyful days: Shabbat and festivals, the new month, Hanukkah and Purim, the whole month of Nisan. When there's a groom in the room in the week after his wedding, or a father whose baby is having his bris that day. Even, strangely, on the fast of Tisha b'Av, because a verse in Lamentations calls that day a mo'ed, an appointed time, the same word used for a festival. Head down on ordinary weekdays; head up on the days marked for joy.
screen: `TACHANUN: PLEADING.` · `FROM FALLING ON THE FACE TO THE ARM.` · `INTO GOD'S HANDS, NOT HUMAN HANDS.` · `LEFT OUT ON JOYFUL DAYS.` · then, large: `LOW AND HONEST.`

segments.voice: If you're at a table or desk, lean forward and rest your forehead on your forearm; if not, just lower your head and let your shoulders drop. From down there, say one honest thing, where you fell short this week or what you're tired of carrying, without arguing with it or fixing it. If you pray, you can say it into God's hands, then sit up slowly when you're ready.
Tachanun. Supplication. The prayer after the Amidah, said with the head down on the arm, and left out on joyful days.
Your line: low and honest. Some words are best said from the low place. See you tomorrow.

597.title: The ark opens
597.hook: the congregation stands as the Torah is carried around and greeted with a kiss
597.howItsDone: On Monday and Thursday mornings, Shabbat, festivals, Rosh Chodesh and fast days, the ark is opened and the congregation stands; the Torah is carried around the synagogue, and people touch its cover with a tallit fringe or prayer book and kiss it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tachanun, the head on the arm. Your line was low and honest. Today, the room stands up again, and the doors at the front swing open.

On Monday and Thursday mornings, on Shabbat, festivals and the new month, the service reaches a moment like a parade in a very small space. Someone pulls back a curtain at the front of the room. The doors behind it open. Everyone stands. A scroll in a velvet cover, or a carved wooden case, is lifted out and carried through the aisles. People reach out as it passes. A woman touches it with the corner of her prayer book. A child is lifted up to kiss it.
screen: `A CURTAIN PULLED BACK.` → `EVERYONE STANDS.` → `A PARADE IN A SMALL SPACE.`

segments.voice: Why those days? The Talmud, in Bava Kamma 82a, starts with a verse: in the wilderness, the people walked three days and found no water. The rabbis read water as Torah, and say the prophets of that generation made sure the people would never again go three days without it: so, a reading on Shabbat, on Monday and on Thursday. Later, the Talmud says, Ezra the scribe added to the system. As the ark opens, many congregations sing a verse Moses said when the ark set out in the wilderness. In the old Jewish translation: "Rise up, O LORD, and let Thine enemies be scattered." Then a line from Isaiah: "for out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem." The cabinet shares its name with that traveling ark: Ashkenazim call it the aron kodesh, the holy ark, and Sephardim often call it the heichal, the palace. The congregation stands while it's open. The Talmud, in Kiddushin, argues: if people rise for those who study the Torah, how much more for the Torah itself. Then the scroll is carried around. People don't usually touch the parchment; they touch the cover with the fringes of their tallit or the edge of a prayer book, and kiss that. In many Sephardi communities, the scroll lives in a hard case and stands upright to be read. The scroll the whole room stood for isn't locked away or kept on a stage. It's brought down the aisles, close enough to touch.

segments.voice: Somewhere in your home is one thing that carries more than its weight: a grandparent's book, a photo, a letter, a ring, a child's first drawing. Stand in front of it if you can, or stand where you are and picture it, still for a moment, the way you'd stand for someone who walked into the room. If you like, touch it gently, the way people touch the scroll.
Aron kodesh. The holy ark: the cabinet whose doors open for the Torah, when the congregation stands and the scroll is carried through the room and kissed.
Your line: stand for the scroll. Honored, and still close enough to touch. Day five hundred ninety-seven, done.

598.title: The pointer
598.hook: the reader follows the words with a silver hand, so the scroll isn't touched
598.howItsDone: During the Torah reading, the reader follows the text with a yad, a pointer ending in a small hand, while gabbaim follow in a printed chumash and correct errors; those called up touch the scroll with a tallit fringe or its cover and kiss it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the aron kodesh opened and the room stood. Your line was stand for the scroll. Today, the scroll is open on the table, and a small silver hand appears.

Here is the job description. Read aloud, in front of a full room, from a page with no punctuation, no vowels, no verse numbers, and no notes on how to sing it. Just columns of black Hebrew letters, written by hand on parchment, in a text the room expects to hear without a single word wrong. And no putting a finger on the line to keep your place. That's the Torah reader's job, week after week. And there's a small tool on the table to help, shaped like a hand.
screen: `NO VOWELS, NO PUNCTUATION.` → `NOT A SINGLE WORD WRONG.` → `A TOOL SHAPED LIKE A HAND.`

segments.voice: It's called a yad: Hebrew for hand. A slim rod, often silver, sometimes wood, ending in a tiny hand with one finger pointing. The reader holds it just above the parchment and moves it word by word. Why not just use a finger? Two reasons. First, the scroll itself is fragile, and treated as holy. Every letter is written by a trained scribe, a sofer, with a quill and special ink, and a smudged or broken letter can make the whole scroll unfit until it's repaired. Hands carry oil and sweat. Second, there's a teaching in the Talmud, in Megillah 32a, that holding a Torah scroll with bare hands is a kind of disrespect. So people touch it with something else: the fringe of a tallit, the cover, or the yad. The yad itself is a custom, not a law spelled out in the Talmud, but today it's a familiar sight at the reading table. Because the scroll has no vowels or musical notes, the reader prepares well ahead. In many synagogues, two people stand on either side, following in a printed book with all the vowels and notes, ready to quietly correct a mistake. And the person called up to bless the reading touches the place with their tallit fringe and kisses it. The yad teaches something without a word. The point isn't the hand. It's what the hand points to.
screen: `YAD: A HAND THAT POINTS.` · `A SMUDGED LETTER, AN UNFIT SCROLL.` · `NO VOWELS, NO NOTES: PREPARED BY HEART.` · `THE POINT IS WHAT IT POINTS TO.` · then, large: `A HAND THAT POINTS.`

segments.voice: Pick up something written, a book, a letter, a page of scripture, even a recipe, and read a few lines slowly, moving your finger or a pen just under each word. Don't let your eyes run ahead of your hand; notice the small words and odd spellings you'd usually skim. If it's a sacred text for you, let the pointing be a kind of respect.

599.title: Lifting the scroll
599.hook: the open scroll is raised high for everyone to see
599.howItsDone: At hagbah, one person lifts the open Torah scroll and turns to show the congregation, who sing V'zot haTorah; in most Ashkenazi communities this follows the reading and in most Sephardi communities it precedes it, and a second person, the golel, rolls and dresses the scroll.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the yad, the silver hand. Your line was a hand that points. Today, the scroll leaves the table and goes up.

A person walks up to the reading table and takes hold of the two wooden rollers of an open Torah scroll. It's heavy, and open several columns wide. They slide it to the edge, bend their knees, and in one motion lift it high overhead, arms spread, the letters facing the room. Then they turn slowly, so everyone can see. Some people stretch out a finger toward it. Some sing. Nobody breathes much until it's safely down.
screen: `TWO WOODEN ROLLERS.` → `LIFTED HIGH, ARMS SPREAD.` → `TURNING SO EVERYONE CAN SEE.`

segments.voice: It's called hagbah, lifting. The lifter raises the scroll open, often wide enough that at least three columns show, and turns so every part of the room can see the writing. A later rabbinic handbook for scribes, tractate Soferim, describes the scroll shown to everyone, men and women, so all could see the letters and bow. As it rises, the congregation sings: this is the Torah that Moses set before the children of Israel. The first half comes from Deuteronomy. In the old Jewish translation: "And this is the law which Moses set before the children of Israel." It echoes a much older scene. When Ezra the scribe gathered the people in Jerusalem, the book of Nehemiah says he opened the book in the sight of all the people, "and when he opened it, all the people stood up." The timing differs. In most Ashkenazi communities, the lifting comes after the reading; in most Sephardi communities, before. Then a second person, the golel, rolls the scroll closed and dresses it again in its cover. The Talmud, in Megillah 32a, gives that rolling a surprising honor: the one who rolls the scroll receives the reward of all the readers. So the text isn't just read to people. It's shown: lifted out of the experts' hands and turned toward everyone, so the whole room can see it's real.

Hagbah. Lifting. The open Torah scroll raised high and turned so everyone in the room can see the writing.
Your line: lift it up. What's held high is meant for the whole room. Day five hundred ninety-nine, done.

600.title: The prophets answer
600.hook: a reading from the prophets follows the Torah on Shabbat and festivals
600.howItsDone: On Shabbat, festivals and fast days the maftir reads the closing verses of the Torah portion and then chants the haftarah from the Prophets, with blessings before and after; many bar and bat mitzvah students chant it as their portion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hagbah, the scroll lifted high for everyone to see. Your line was lift it up. Today, once the scroll is rolled closed, a second reading begins.

For months, a melody has leaked through a bedroom door: a teenager practicing, stopping, starting the same line again. Then the Saturday comes. The family fills the front rows, the voice cracks once on a high note, and the whole room holds its breath until the last word. Ask what that teenager was chanting, and the answer is often: my haftarah. Ask what a haftarah is, and why it comes after the Torah, and the room may go quiet. It isn't from the Torah scroll at all.
screen: `A MELODY THROUGH A BEDROOM DOOR.` → `MY HAFTARAH.` → `NOT FROM THE TORAH SCROLL.`

segments.voice: On Shabbat, festivals and fast days, after the Torah reading, one more person is called up, the maftir. They read the last few verses of the portion again, then a passage from the Prophets, from books like Isaiah, Jeremiah, Samuel or Kings. That passage is the haftarah. The word comes from a root meaning to conclude, to complete. It isn't half of anything; it's the closing reading. Each haftarah is chosen to answer the Torah portion. When the Torah tells of Moses sending spies into the land, the haftarah tells of Joshua sending spies to Jericho. Around the summer fast of Tisha b'Av, the pattern takes over the calendar: three haftarot of warning before the fast, then seven of comfort after it. The first of the seven opens Isaiah forty. In the old Jewish translation: "Comfort ye, comfort ye My people, saith your God." Why read the Prophets at all? A popular explanation, written down in the Middle Ages, says that when a foreign king banned Torah reading, Jews read matching passages from the Prophets instead. Historians aren't sure that's how it began; the Mishnah already lays down rules for the reading. Either way, the shape says something. The Torah speaks, and the prophets answer: later voices taking up the same story, centuries on, asking what it means now.
screen: `THE MAFTIR READS THE PROPHETS.` · `HAFTARAH: THE CONCLUDING READING.` · `CHOSEN TO ANSWER THE PORTION.` · `COMFORT YE, MY PEOPLE.` · then, large: `THE PROPHETS ANSWER.`

segments.voice: If you have a Bible nearby, open to Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos or Micah, anywhere, and read one line slowly; if not, take today's line: comfort ye, comfort ye My people. Ask who needed to hear it the day it was first said, and let one face come to mind who might need it now.
Haftarah. The concluding reading. A passage from the Prophets read after the Torah, chosen to answer it.

601.title: Prayers for others
601.hook: blessings for the sick, the community and the country
601.howItsDone: During the Torah service, Mi Sheberach blessings are said for those called up, for the sick, whose names are added aloud or whispered to the leader, and for the congregation; many synagogues also say prayers for the country and for the State of Israel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the haftarah, the Prophets answering the Torah. Your line was comfort after the warning. Today, the prayers said around the open scroll, for other people.

While the Torah lies open on the table, there's a pause between readings. Someone walks up to the leader and whispers a name. Then another. Then a list on a scrap of paper. A neighbor's husband after surgery. A cousin's newborn. A friend in rehab. The leader starts a short prayer, and when it reaches the gap, the names pour in, sometimes for a full minute. In some congregations, people simply stand and say them aloud, one after another, until the room goes quiet again.
screen: `A NAME WHISPERED TO THE LEADER.` → `A LIST ON A SCRAP OF PAPER.` → `THE NAMES POUR IN.`

segments.voice: The prayer begins Mi sheberach avoteinu: may the One who blessed our ancestors, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and in many communities Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, bless this person. It's a frame, and almost anything can go in it. There's a Mi Sheberach for each person called up to the Torah. One for the sick, asking for complete healing of body and spirit, where the names from that scrap of paper go. One for the whole congregation and everyone who gives to it and serves it. One for a new baby, one for a couple about to marry. Many synagogues also pray for the country and its leaders, and in many communities for the State of Israel and those who defend it. Praying for the government has deep roots. The prophet Jeremiah writes to the exiles in Babylon, in the old Jewish translation: "seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray unto the LORD for it; for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace." Not Jerusalem, the city they lost. Babylon, the city that took them captive. In Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Chanina, deputy of the priests, says to pray for the welfare of the government, because without it, people would swallow one another alive. In recent decades the songwriter Debbie Friedman wrote a sung version of the prayer for healing, and some synagogues now sing it instead. The frame stays the same: the blessing that reached our ancestors, asked for someone else.
screen: `MAY THE ONE WHO BLESSED OUR ANCESTORS.` · `FOR THE SICK, THE CALLED UP, THE NEW.` · `SEEK THE PEACE OF THE CITY.` · `PRAY FOR THE GOVERNMENT'S WELFARE.` · then, large: `PRAY FOR THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Picture the place you live: the main street, the school, the hospital, the people you pass without knowing their names, and the people who run it, the ones you voted for and the ones you didn't. 602.title: Our duty to praise
602.hook: once a High Holy Day prayer, now said at the end of every service
602.howItsDone: Aleinu is said standing at the end of the morning, afternoon and evening services, and many people bend the knees and bow at the line about bending the knee; on the High Holy Days many congregations kneel and prostrate fully during it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mi Sheberach, the blessing for the sick, the community and the country. Your line was pray for the city. Today, the prayer that closes almost every service.

Morning, afternoon or evening, the last few minutes of a synagogue service tend to sound alike. People stand. The tune picks up. And at one line, the room bends its knees and bows, together. It sounds like an ending that was always there. Historians say otherwise. For a long stretch, this prayer belonged to Rosh Hashanah, the New Year, in the solemn season of the High Holy Days. Then, sometime in the Middle Ages, it moved out of the High Holy Days and into every single day.
screen: `THE WHOLE ROOM BOWS.` → `ONCE A NEW YEAR PRAYER.` → `NOW EVERY DAY.`

segments.voice: Its first word is aleinu: it is upon us, it is our duty. The opening says, roughly, it is our duty to praise the Master of all, to give greatness to the one who formed the world. Then the bowing line: and we bend the knee and bow and give thanks before the King of kings. That's when people bow. Where did it come from? Tradition credits Joshua. Some scholars connect it with the sage Rav in Babylonia, who is said to have arranged the Rosh Hashanah prayers about God's kingship; Aleinu opens that section. On the High Holy Days it keeps its old drama: in many synagogues the cantor, and sometimes everyone, kneels and lowers all the way to the floor, a posture the rest of the year's prayers don't ask for. The second paragraph turns outward, toward a hope: a day when the world will be repaired under the kingship of God. The Hebrew phrase there, l'taken olam, to repair the world, is one of the roots of the modern words tikkun olam. It ends with a verse from Zechariah, in the old Jewish translation: "And the LORD shall be King over all the earth; in that day shall the LORD be One, and His name one." So the prayer moves in two steps: our duty to praise, right now, on our knees, and the hope that one day the whole world will join in. The service ends holding both.
screen: `ALEINU: IT IS UPON US.` · `WE BEND THE KNEE AND BOW.` · `FROM ROSH HASHANAH TO EVERY DAY.` · `TO REPAIR THE WORLD.` · then, large: `OUR DUTY TO PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Stand, if you can, and if you pray, say the opening in your own language: it is our duty to praise. At we bend the knee and bow, do just that, knees soft, a bow from the waist, then come back up slowly and stand a moment, letting your body remember what it just said.
Aleinu. It is upon us. The prayer of duty and hope that closes the service, with a bow in the middle.
Your line: bow now, and hope later. A week of Tachanun, the ark opening, the yad, lifting the scroll, the haftarah, Mi Sheberach and Aleinu. That's day six hundred two.
